entities.name: The Motherland Calls
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Motherland Calls, an imposing monument located in Volgograd, Russia, represents a pivotal symbol of Soviet resilience and valor during World War II, specifically commemorating the Battle of Stalingrad, which lasted from August 1942 to February 1943. Designed by architect Nikolai Nikitin and unveiled in 1967, this colossal statue stands 85 meters tall, making it one of the tallest statues in the world at the time. It serves as a testament to the profound sacrifices made by Soviet soldiers and civilians alike during one of the war's deadliest confrontations, marking a significant turning point in the Eastern Front of World War II.

The creation of The Motherland Calls was initiated in the context of post-war Soviet nationalism, which sought to reinforce collective memory and honor the heroic struggles of the Red Army. Construction began in 1959 and involved thousands of workers and engineers, symbolizing the industrial might and ideological resolve of the Soviet Union during the Cold War era. The statue's design, which features a woman wielding a sword, embodies the spirit of the motherland and has become an enduring icon of Russian patriotism and resilience.

In terms of legacy, The Motherland Calls not only transformed the landscape of Volgograd but also influenced memorial architecture and national identity across post-Soviet states. It has been a site of pilgrimage for veterans and a venue for commemorative events, notably the annual celebrations of the victory in the Great Patriotic War. The statue continues to inspire art and literature, reflecting the ongoing narrative of war, sacrifice, and national pride in Russian culture.
